common_name: Prairie Charm Itoh Peony (Gold Medal Pale Yellow Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Prairie Charm is an Itoh hybrid bred by Roger Anderson that earned the American Peony Society Gold Medal, bearing large, semi-double, pale creamy-yellow flowers marked with fine red flares near the center and set off by a boss of golden stamens. It typically opens between the main flush of herbaceous peonies and the earlier tree peonies, extending the garden's peony season, and its sturdy, well-branched stems hold the blooms upright without staking. Deeply cut, dark green foliage stays clean and attractive through summer, and like other intersectional hybrids the plant dies back to the ground each fall rather than persisting as a woody shrub.

common_name: Cytherea Itoh Peony (Coral-Pink and Yellow Intersectional Peony)

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1-2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Cytherea is a Roger Anderson Itoh hybrid bearing large, semi-double flowers that open coral pink at the petal edges and warm to a soft yellow blush toward the center, a color blend distinct from the more common clear yellows and pinks in the Itoh group. Its strong, woody-based stems support the heavy blooms without staking, and the deeply lobed foliage remains glossy and disease-free well past bloom. Like other intersectional hybrids it combines tree-peony flower form with the reliable winter die-back and cold hardiness of herbaceous types, and resents frequent division or transplanting.

Going Bananas is an Itoh hybrid bred by Don Hollingsworth, producing heavily ruffled, semi-double flowers in deep, saturated yellow with a ring of red flares surrounding the center, a bolder color break than paler yellow Itohs such as Bartzella. Strong, self-supporting stems carry the large blooms without staking, and the deeply cut, glossy foliage holds up cleanly through summer heat. It shares the die-back-to-the-ground habit and broad soil tolerance typical of intersectional hybrids and should be left undisturbed once established.

common_name: Shintenchi Tree Peony (Japanese Semi-Double Pink and White Tree Peony)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in early to mid fall in deep, humus-rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial afternoon shade, setting a grafted union 4-6 inches below the soil surface to encourage the scion to form its own roots.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Shintenchi is a traditional Japanese tree peony cultivar whose name translates roughly as 'new heaven and earth,' bearing large, semi-double flowers that open soft pink and fade toward near-white at the ruffled petal margins, centered on a prominent cluster of golden stamens. It forms a full, rounded shrub with broad, deeply lobed foliage that provides good structure after the mid-spring bloom period ends. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

directions: Plant in deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since tree peonies resent being moved once established. Yachiyotsubaki, a name evoking an 'everlasting camellia,' is a traditional Japanese tree peony bearing dense, semi-double, deep crimson-red flowers whose rounded, overlapping petals give the bloom a camellia-like form rather than the looser, ruffled shape typical of many tree peony cultivars. The compact flowers are held well above the deeply cut, dark green foliage on a full, rounded shrub in mid spring. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

Yao Huang, meaning 'Yao's Yellow,' is one of the two most celebrated tree peony cultivars in Chinese horticultural history, recorded in Luoyang peony literature dating back to the Song dynasty and traditionally paired with the purple 'Wei Zi' as the classic yellow-and-purple standard of the ancient Luoyang gardens. It bears fully double, pale golden-yellow flowers with a dense, ball-shaped form on a vigorous, upright shrub. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

Wei Zi, meaning 'Wei's Purple,' is the historic counterpart to the yellow 'Yao Huang' among the most famous tree peony cultivars of ancient Luoyang, celebrated in classical Chinese peony writing for its rich, deep purple-violet, fully double flowers held on a sturdy, spreading shrub. The heavy, densely petaled blooms open in mid spring above broad, dark green foliage. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.

Er Qiao, meaning 'Two Beauties' after a pair of legendary sisters from Chinese history, is a long-cultivated cultivar noted for producing flowers of two distinct colors, typically white and pink or rose, on the same plant and sometimes within the same bloom. Its large, loosely double flowers open in mid spring on a vigorous, well-branched shrub with broad, deeply cut foliage. Give full sun where summers are mild but afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot, humid climates, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the prior year's wood.
